Root semi-hardwood cuttings in spring or set out container plants once the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun. 'Hardy Red' produces deep red single flowers in loose clusters from late spring through fall, but its real distinction is a root system bred to survive winters that kill lesser oleanders outright, resprouting reliably even after a hard freeze burns the top growth to the ground. This makes it a dependable choice for colder pockets of zone 8 and protected sites in zone 7b where standard red-flowered oleanders struggle to persist. Tolerates heat, drought, salt spray, and poor soil once established.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in spring or set out container plants once the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun; the pink-flowered counterpart to 'Hardy Red', selected for the same extra root cold-hardiness that suits it to zone 7b-8 gardens.

directions: WARNING: ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE HIGHLY TOXIC IF INGESTED — site it away from grazing animals and small children, and never burn the prunings. Root semi-hardwood cuttings in spring or set out container plants once the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun. 'Hardy Pink' bears clear, medium-pink single flowers in dense terminal clusters from late spring into fall on a vigorous, upright shrub, and like its sibling selection 'Hardy Red' it was chosen for root systems that survive winter cold well beyond what most oleanders tolerate, resprouting from the base after freezes that would kill a less hardy selection outright. It performs equally well as a screening hedge or a large specimen shrub and needs only occasional thinning of old canes to stay dense from the ground up.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in spring or set out container plants once the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun; a historic California-bred double-flowered selection that stays more compact than full-size single-flowered oleanders.

directions: WARNING: ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE HIGHLY TOXIC IF INGESTED — keep it well away from grazing animals and small children, and never burn the wood. Root semi-hardwood cuttings in spring or set out container plants once the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun. Named for the Roeding family of Fresno, California nursery fame, 'Mrs. Roeding' is prized for its densely packed, fully double flowers in a soft salmon-pink that give each bloom cluster an almost rose-like fullness, appearing from late spring through fall on a more restrained, rounded frame than most full-size oleanders. Its moderate size makes it a good fit for a foundation planting or large mixed border rather than a screening hedge, and it shares the species' indifference to heat, drought, salt spray, and poor soil.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in spring or set out container plants once the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun; grown for its ruffled, deep ruby-red flowers on a medium-sized, upright shrub.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings in spring or set out container plants once the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun. 'Ruby Lace' stands out among red oleanders for its distinctively ruffled, almost frilled petal edges, which give each deep ruby-red single flower a textured, lacy appearance rather than the flat-faced form typical of most oleanders, blooming heavily from late spring through fall. It grows into a medium, upright shrub well suited to a sunny border or informal screen, and like the rest of the species it tolerates heat, drought, salt spray, and poor soil with little care once established.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in spring or set out container plants once the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun; one of the few soft-yellow-flowered oleander selections, valued for a flower color rarely seen in the species.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings in spring or set out container plants once the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun. 'Isle of Capri' bears pale, buttery-yellow single flowers in loose clusters from late spring through fall, a color rarely found among the reds, pinks, and whites that dominate the oleander market, giving it particular value as an accent among other oleander selections or as a distinctive stand-alone specimen. It grows into a moderately sized, well-branched shrub and shares the species' tolerance for heat, drought, salt spray, and lean soil.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or set out container-grown plants in spring after frost danger has passed, in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; the arching canes benefit from a partly shaded site that spares the foliage from harsh afternoon sun.

directions: Root stem cuttings or set out container-grown plants in spring after frost danger has passed, in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Red cestrum is grown for its dense, drooping clusters of tubular, dusky rose-red to reddish-purple flowers that weigh down its long, arching canes for much of the year in mild climates, followed by round, shiny purple-black berries; unlike night-blooming jessamine, its fragrance is faint and the flowers open by day, drawing hummingbirds rather than moths. Its lax, fountain-like habit makes it useful as an informal border shrub or trained loosely against a fence or wall where its cascading branches can be shown off. As with other cestrums, the berries are toxic if ingested, so keep it away from small children and pets, and prune after flowering to control its sprawling growth.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or set out container-grown plants in spring after all frost danger has passed, in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; give it protection from hard freezes since it is more cold-tender than most other landscape cestrums.

directions: Root stem cuttings or set out container-grown plants in spring after frost danger has passed, in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Orange cestrum carries clusters of bright orange, tubular flowers almost continuously in warm weather, a striking color unmatched by any other cestrum grown in Gulf Coast gardens, and it will rebloom repeatedly through the growing season with only light deadheading of spent clusters. It grows into a loose, sprawling shrub best given some support or occasional pinching to keep it from becoming leggy, and it draws hummingbirds and butterflies reliably wherever it is planted. As with related cestrums, its berries are toxic if ingested, so it should not be sited near small children, pets, or grazing animals.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; this compact selection is especially well suited to containers and small foundation beds where the standard species would grow too large.

directions: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. 'Floribunda' is a naturally dwarf, densely branched selection of yesterday-today-tomorrow that stays under 4 feet, making it far more practical than the standard species for foundation plantings, mixed borders, and large patio containers, while still producing the same violet-to-lavender-to-white color-change flowers in unusually heavy flushes for its small size. Its compact form needs little pruning to stay tidy, and its shallow root system makes it easy to grow in pots that can be moved to shelter during cold snaps in zone 9. All parts of the plant, especially the berries, are toxic if ingested and pose a particular hazard to dogs.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; this Amazonian species is more cold-tender than the common landscape brunfelsias and needs frost protection or container culture in zone 9.

directions: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade. Native to the western Amazon basin, Brunfelsia grandiflora carries the same yesterday-today-tomorrow color progression from violet-purple through lavender to white, but on noticeably larger flowers and a much larger, more tree-like frame than the compact garden brunfelsias, eventually reaching small-tree proportions where winters stay frost-free. It blooms heaviest in spring with sporadic flowering through the warm months, and its size makes it best used as a large specimen or informal screen in sheltered, part-shaded sites rather than a foundation planting. All parts are toxic if ingested and the species has a long history of use and misuse as a psychoactive plant in traditional Amazonian medicine, underscoring the need to keep it away from children and pets.
